prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, in which atoms trapped at a magic wavelength allow many atoms to be interrogated without a light shift, bringing optical timekeeping to a fractional uncertainty near 10^-18

statement.case_for: I keep optical lattice clocks as my preferred configuration, and after the full first round I can say more precisely why. The physical idea is a cancellation: at the magic wavelength the light that holds the atoms shifts the two clock levels equally, so the trap does not disturb the transition, and thousands of neutral atoms can be probed at once. That is a different problem from the one solved by the comb in 2005 (a ruler for optical frequencies) or by single-ion control in 2012 (one well-isolated quantum system). The claim has then been tested in the way I trust most: independent clocks in Japan, the United States, France, Germany and China have been compared directly and agree at the 10^-18 level, and the same instruments are already used for real questions such as gravitational redshift over centimetres and limits on variation of constants. The two-name credit follows the invention (Katori) and the demonstrated record performance (Ye) and fits the three-laureate rule without any painful carving. I also want to be fair to the case for B033. The arguments of Mehlig and Eriksson that a quantitative continuum-model prediction was followed by a sharp experimental test, and then by wide reproduction, are strong, and they moved me on one point (see responses): the discovery of the correlated phases does not depend on the pairing mechanism. I still prefer B026 because the verified, cross-laboratory character of the result is, to me, unusually complete, but I regard B033 as a legitimate first choice for this committee and not a weaker one that I would resist.
statement.case_against: The strongest objection to my own choice is novelty. A sceptic can say that lattice clocks are a spectacular refinement of precision metrology that two earlier prizes already recognised, and that nothing about the physics is a surprise in the sense that high-harmonic generation or flat bands at a magic angle were surprises. I think the magic-wavelength idea answers part of that, but not all of it: the discovery content is narrower than a new field of correlated matter, and the breadth of follow-on science is smaller than for moire materials. I also discount my own enthusiasm, since atomic physics is where I am least critical. Finally, several contributors (Lemonde and colleagues, Ludlow, Bloom, Derevianko on theory) have real claims that a two-name credit leaves aside, and the first-demonstration chronology is from my recollection and has not been checked here. Against B033 itself, the open pairing mechanism and the dependence of the phase diagram on twist-angle disorder still make me ask whether the experimental claim is fully pinned down, though I now see this as a question about how sharply the citation is worded, not about whether the phenomenon is real.

responses.point: Mehlig answered my maturity worry about B033 by saying the discovery claimed is the existence and tunability of correlated insulating and superconducting states, which many independent groups have reproduced across graphene multilayers and other moire systems, and not a theory of pairing.
responses.response: I accept that distinction, and it changes how I weigh my reservation. In my first-round statement I treated the open pairing mechanism and sample dependence as a reason to call B033 somewhat early. If the citation is drawn narrowly around the prediction and the discovery of the correlated and superconducting states, the claim stands on reproduction by several laboratories and does not require the mechanism, much as the field of conventional superconductors was recognised before every question about the cuprates was settled. What I still ask of the B033 supporters is a common standard: I want the citation to avoid any wording about why the phases occur, and I would like us to say plainly that device-to-device variation is large. On B037, I take your point that it is a Hubbard-model simulator whose headline results are the Mott transition and microscopy, and that five credited names cannot be carved cleanly. That is why I am dropping it from my alternatives.

responses.point: Danielsson says he does not want B026 ahead of B033 on maturity grounds, doubts that the redefinition of the second has happened, and asks, in effect, what distinguishes my confidence in clocks from my caution about moire graphene.
responses.response: The distinction I would defend is the standard of independent confirmation, and I am happy to apply it to both. For clocks, several laboratories built their own systems with different atoms and different traps, and they agree numerically at 10^-18 when compared, which is a direct test of the quantity that is claimed. For B033, many groups have reproduced the existence of correlated insulators and superconductivity, which I accept as the discovery, but the quantitative phase diagram differs from sample to sample, so the confirmation is of the phenomenon, not yet of the numbers. Both are mature in the sense that matters for a prize; the clocks are further along on quantitative agreement and B033 is further along on novelty. On the redefinition of the second, I agree with you that it has not happened, and I would not cite it as support. Prizes should rest on what has been shown. That is why I do not see it as a reason to wait either.

responses.point: Kroll proposes drawing the clock citation narrowly around the magic-wavelength lattice and many-atom interrogation, avoiding Hall, Hansch or ion-clock names, and does not think waiting for the redefinition is needed.
responses.response: I agree and I have tightened the citation accordingly. I would add one caution that I think we should state aloud: the pre-2005 and 2012 prizes honoured the comb and ion control, and our citation must not read as a statement that lattice clocks are simply the next clock. The invention is the magic-wavelength condition applied to many neutral atoms. I also ask you to consider what you and I would do if the committee settles on B033: you rank it as your first alternative, and I rank it as mine, so our fallback is the same. On your point that experimental disorder makes credit harder for B033, I would now put it more cautiously than I did, since Mehlig's argument that the discovery is the existence of the phases is reasonable. I do not move off B026, but I do not claim that clock-to-clock comparisons settle which discovery is more important.

responses.point: Eriksson moved his third seat from Andrei to Bistritzer, argues that B033 opened a new field while clocks are an improvement of an established measurement, and says B026 is the natural partner if the committee prefers a split prize but would more likely be a separate year.
responses.response: Your ordering argument is the fair statement of the disagreement between us, and I do not think it is a mistake. Where I would push back is on calling the clock an improvement of an established measurement: a gain of several orders of magnitude from a new physical idea is, in my own experience of atomic physics, how a field changes, and clocks at this level now measure height differences by gravity. I take the point that B033 is broader. On the split-prize idea I do not think it is available this year: B033 with its supporters' trio takes the three seats and B026 needs two, so a two-part configuration would exceed the limit of three people, and I will not propose it. I also found your note about lattice relaxation useful. It makes me want the B033 citation to describe the prediction as a continuum-model one and not to imply that the quantitative band structure is settled.

responses.point: Pearce now prefers B033 over his own opening first choice IceCube, argues that the prediction-plus-experiment structure gives a clean three-person prize, and admits that the pairing mechanism is open and that Andrei is a credible fourth claim.
responses.response: I respect that you moved off your own first choice because of the arguments and not a vote count, and I would do the same if I thought the arguments pointed that way. On the Andrei question, which the chair has asked about directly, I cannot resolve it from memory: as I understand it, her group reported flat-band and Van Hove singularity signatures by STM in twisted layers before 2018, which is an indication of flat-band physics but not the discovery of the correlated insulator and superconducting phases. I would therefore say the defensible core is the prediction and the discovery of those phases, and the committee should record that the earlier STM work is real. I would be uncomfortable calling it secondary without checking the dating, and I do not claim the checking has been done. I also agree with you and the others that B024 should not advance with a single credited name.

uncertainties: Whether the committee judges lattice clocks to be a distinct discovery from the 2005 and 2012 prizes or a refinement of recognised metrology. I believe the magic-wavelength idea is distinct, but I judge this from inside the field.

Whether B033 is better supported than B026 once the common standard for independent confirmation is applied. I now think the phenomenon is secure and the question is mainly the third name (Bistritzer or Andrei) and the exact wording of the citation.
The first-demonstration chronology for lattice clocks (Katori, Takamoto, Ye, Lemonde and others) is from my recollection and has not been verified here.
For B009, whether Mele or Hasan belongs beside Kane and Molenkamp. I proposed Mele in my opening but cannot resolve it, and the missing Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang HgTe prediction troubles me.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict has arisen in round 1 that changes my earlier disclosure. I collaborate closely with Anne L'Huillier (2023 laureate) and the Lund and ETH attosecond groups, but none of them is credited on the shortlist. I have no known ties to Katori or Ye, to the Munich, Harvard or Zurich cold-atom groups, or to the condensed-matter candidates. I am an atomic theorist and share a general field with the lattice-clock community, which I disclose again as a possible bias toward B026 and not as a recusal issue. Kroll and I both prefer B026, and I want it recorded that our agreement comes from the arguments exchanged and not from coordination.
